title: Home to the porch
hookLine: after seven visits, a deeper look at the school this path quotes most
carry: the fence, the soil, the fruit

cards: You sat in a Hindu home with a lamp and a flower, took refuge with Buddhists, argued over a page with Jewish students, walked with Christians and with Catholics, fasted with Muslims, and ate on the floor with Sikhs.
Each time you were a guest, and a good guest goes home. So where is home on this path?
If you've walked it from the start, you know: the voice that argued with itself under the blankets, the enslaved teacher, the man who wrote letters about time. Home is the Stoa.

teach.b: Back on day twenty-seven you met the porch itself: the Stoa Poikile, the painted colonnade on the edge of the market in Athens, where, Diogenes Laërtius tells us, a shipwrecked merchant named Zeno started teaching.
The school was named after the porch. Since then this path has leaned on three writers of the Roman era more than anyone: Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.
This month goes deeper, so it helps to know the shape of the whole school first.
Stoics split philosophy into three parts: logic, how to think clearly; physics, how the world works; and ethics, how to live.
Diogenes Laërtius, who collected their lives, reports that they liked to picture it as a fenced orchard. Logic is the fence. Physics is the soil and the trees.
Ethics is the fruit. You can't have the fruit without the rest. Now the honest part.
Almost everything the early Greek Stoics wrote is lost. Chrysippus, the school's great systematizer, is said to have written more than seven hundred books. Not one survives whole.

teach.h: WHAT'S LEFT IS ROMAN AND PRACTICAL.
teach.b: What's left are fragments quoted by other people, often by critics.
The Stoicism that reaches us whole is the late Roman version, practical and personal, written by men who were trying to live it.
So the next weeks go in order: what the Stoics said is good, how they saw feelings, their picture of the world, and then the Stoics honestly, with their blind spots.
First, where Epictetus starts his Handbook, in George Long's 1877 translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not."

how: People who practice Stoicism today often keep a short line from Epictetus, Seneca or Marcus Aurelius close by and reread it in the morning or when something goes wrong.

practice: Come back to that line slowly, the way you'd come back to a house you grew up in: of things some are in our power, and others are not. Let one thing from this week drift up, and notice which side of the line it sits on.
Don't fix it; just see where it lands.
